title: Experiment Orchestration Wizard — notes and wireframe annotations
body:
Purpose:
Quick working notes for the Experiment Orchestration Wizard (EOW) — a guided console flow to create canaries, A/B experiments, and automatic fallback policies. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: sketches, microcopy, interaction edge cases, and a prioritized backlog for the next two sprints.

Context and goals:
- Problem: teams create rollouts via YAML or scattered UI pages. Hard to get right: traffic ramps, inference variants, fallback chains.
- EOW objective: make a single path that lets engineers and product managers set up safe experiments quickly while exposing advanced knobs for power users.
- Success metrics: time-to-first-traffic < 10 minutes for typical canary, % of rollouts created via wizard, and reduction in rollback incidents tied to rollout misconfigurations.

Primary personas:
- ML Engineer (fast, needs control): wants precise traffic schedules, seed prompts for eval, and deterministic rollback triggers.
- Product Manager (safe defaults): needs simple A/B split, compare quality and cost estimates, non-technical microcopy.
- Platform Engineer (compliance): needs audit metadata, pinning, and ability to require canary approvals.

High-level flow (wizard steps):
1) Quick-select: Template (Canary / A/B / Gradual rollout / Blue-Green). Short description and expected duration.
2) Targeting & Scope: routes, model versions, metadata tags, traffic fraction selectors. Preview of affected endpoints.
3) Traffic schedule: slider + timeline editor. Presets (fast, recommended, conservative). Option for manual step schedule (time + percentage).
4) Quality checks: attach eval sets or pick from recent evals. Quick-run sanity check (sample 50 requests).
5) Fallbacks & Circuit breakers: build chain of fallback strategies (auto-fallback to cheaper model, geographic fallback, degrade to cached response).
6) Approval & Notifications: add approvers, Slack/email notifications, and require approval gating.
7) Launch summary & dry-run: cost estimate, latency delta estimate, and preview traffic simulation.

Wireframe annotation highlights (sketch-level):
- Stepper (left rail) with collapsed summaries for each step; inline status markers (green check / warning / action required).
- Traffic timeline has drag handles and optional second-dimension for expected latency at each segment. Hover reveals estimated cost delta.
- Fallback composer is a mini-flow editor: node-based canvas with simple nodes (model-variant, region, cached-response, manual-intervention). Default ordering: model-variant -> region -> cached-response -> manual.
- Microcopy: emphasize safety: "If this canary fails a quality check, remove traffic and notify the owners immediately." Use short bullets and examples for PMs.

Microcopy experiments (short):
- Canary preset description: "Seed a small % of real traffic to a new model version so we can validate behavior with low risk."
- Automatic fallback label: "Fallback to: (cheapest compatible model) — triggers when 5xx rate > 2% for 3 minutes."
- Dry-run CTA: "Simulate launch" (non-destructive) and follow-up: "Start canary" (destructive).

Edge cases and gotchas noted during grooming:
- Metric drift detection: when linking an eval set, need to state whether the platform will auto-evaluate incoming traffic or only sample. Default should be sampling with option to enable continuous eval (explicit).
- Overlapping rollouts: if a route already has an active experiment, present blocking or merge options. Merge flow is complex — roll to backlog if timeboxed.
- Campaign collisions across regions (two teams targeting same route in different regions): propose per-region scoping and conflict detection.
- Long-lived canaries: surfaced in a dedicated dashboard to avoid neglect. Warn when canary > 72 hours.

Fallback policy details (composer behavior):
- Simple default chain: fallback to pinned cheaper quantized variant -> fallback to regional replica -> fallback to cached response -> route to manual mode.
- Each node supports: trigger conditions (latency p95 > X ms, error rate > Y, cost per 1k tokens > Z), cooldown, and throttle rules.
- Composer micro-interactions: double-click node to edit trigger, drag to reorder, ctrl+drag to duplicate.

Backlog (prioritized):
1) MVP wizard UI + templates (2-week sprint): core steps, traffic schedule slider, default fallback chain.
2) Eval integration: quick-scan sample runner + result UI (2 sprints).
3) Node-based fallback composer (experimental): MVP canvas with 4 node types (3 sprints).
4) Merge/conflict resolution flows and invitations for cross-team experiments (2 sprints).
5) Advanced RBAC & approval gates + audit export (ongoing).

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default triggers for auto-fallback: conservative out-of-the-box (e.g., 5xx > 1% for 2 minutes) or permissive? Recommendation: conservative to reduce silent failovers until we gather data.
- How many rollout presets should we ship? Suggest 3: Quick Canary, Staged A/B, Full Ramp.
- Should dry-run run a shadowed evaluation against production traffic (privacy concerns)? Consider offering "sampled shadow" with injection only if customer opts in.

Short checklist before next review:
- [ ] Create hi-fi mockups for steps 2 (Targeting) and 5 (Fallback composer).
- [ ] Wire up quick-scan eval runner to show sample results in wizard.
- [ ] Draft copy for approval gating emails and Slack messages.
- [ ] Author acceptance criteria for ROLL-412 and link to SLO docs.

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep default UX over-explanatory for PMs; power users can collapse help.
- Watch language around "auto-fallback" — customers worry about silent cost increases if fallback goes to more expensive model. Always show cost delta.
- Consider a "what changed" diff in launch summary comparing baseline model outputs on sample prompts. Useful for PM signoff.

Appendix: quick sketches pointers
- Sketch A: stepper + timeline on single-screen (see Confluence linked).
- Sketch B: fallback composer canvas, includes node palette and node inspectors.
- Sketch C: dry-run simulation heatmap (traffic vs. latency vs. errors).

Next meeting: review hi-fi mockups with SRE and Applied ML (Marcus, Lina). Goal: finalize triggers and default presets.

-- Aditi
